newsitem.title: GREECE: GREECE FACES WEEK OVER STRIKES OVER ECON POLICIES.
newsitem.headline: GREECE FACES WEEK OVER STRIKES OVER ECON POLICIES.

text.p: Prime Minister Costas Simitis, struggling to cope with a farmers' road blockade in its third week, faces a strike wave across Greece this week to protest against his economic policies.

Farmers, who have blocked national roads for 18 days, threaten to drive their tractors to the capital while public servants, teachers, doctors and diplomats, strike during the five-day parliament debate on the budget starting on Tuesday.

The 1997 budget, aimed at setting the course for Greece to join the European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 2001, cuts state hiring, abolishes most tax exemptions and imposes a string of new taxes.
Simitis, whose budget has been described as the toughest in 15 years, has said "no" to any workers' group asking for more money. Opposition to his economic policies is growing even in his government.

For the first time since winning elections in September he is accused by labour unions of being arrogant and indifferent to the problems of the average Greek, and a "Brussels servant" by the opposition press.
"We should not base our national policy on the blackmail: Maastricht or catastrophy," said Simitis' education minister Gerassimos Arsenis. "The people can't be motivated by such dilemmas."

Simitis was expected to hold his third special cabinet meeting in two weeks on Monday to face the farmers' revolt. Defense Minister Akis Tsohatzopoulos, the government's number two, urged him to meet with the farmers and discuss their problems.

The farmers, pressing for cheaper fuel and state subsidies for their products, have set up five blocks with thousands of tractors along the main north-south highway and vow to continue the seizure over the Christamas holidays.
The blockade has caused millions of dollars in damages to industry, hoteliers and export firms but Simitis has rejected all calls for a compromise.
"If you satisfy the demands of one group then you have to satisfy the demands of everybody else as well, and this will simply destroy the economy," a senior government official told Reuters.
Simitis, a staunch pro-European law and economics professor, has said sacrifices are needed to converge the Greek economy with those of its EU partners.
The budget, which goes on vote in parliament next Saturday, will yield the state next year about $4 billion from the extra taxes and spending cuts.

"The vote on the budget is seen as a vote of confidence to the government. The prime minister has made this clear to all our deputies in parliament. The economic policy is one way towards Europe," the government official said.

Greece's two biggest labour confederations have called a one-day nationwide strike on Tuesday and smaller strikes with daily rallies to the parliament are scheduled throughout the week. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
